# Introduction

## Why R?

-   R is an impressive, do-it-all software: loading spatial datasets, to fitting models, analyzing patterns, and creating publication-quality maps and plots.
-   **reproducibility** of data summaries and statistical analyses.
-   **Automation**: automates repetitive or mundane data processing tasks.
-   **Open-source and free**: constant updates contributed by scientists worldwide.

::: notes
This introductory lab is a foundation for students who have not used R often, or who want to review the basics of data and spatial data structures. Everything in this deck runs in the browser, so nobody needs a working local install on day one.
:::

## R Packages

-   **R packages (libraries)**: bundles of functions, data, and documentation that extend R's capabilities.
-   Spatial packages are catalogued on the CRAN Task View: *Analysis of Spatial Data*.
    -   The two R spatial packages we lean on all semester:
    -   **`sf`**: mostly for vector data (points, lines, polygons)
    -   **`terra`**: mostly for raster data (grids, stacks)
-   Model fitting and post-processing
    -   **`Nimble`** and **`coda`**
-   A few other occasional packages

::: notes
Note that sf and terra have replaced the older sp and raster packages; sp was retired in 2023 and raster is in maintenance mode only.
:::

## Getting Help in R

-   To view documentation for any loaded function, use `help()` or `?`:

```{r}
?runif
help(runif)
```

-   `help(package = "sf")` lists every function in a package.
-   `??aggregate` runs a fuzzy search.
-   Online resources are enormous. The **R-sig-geo** mailing list is invaluable for spatial questions, and pasting an error message into a search engine solves most problems in one step.
-   The elephant in the room: GenAI

::: notes
In R you never have to memorise code. Help pages document the expected inputs (arguments) and the returned value. In r the help page prints as plain text rather than opening a formatted panel.
:::

# Spatial Data in R

## Two Data Types

-   **Vector** data represent discrete features with coordinates: **points** (nest sites, camera stations), **lines** (streams, roads, GPS tracks), **polygons** (home ranges, park boundaries, watersheds). Handled by **`sf`**, class `sf` / `sfc`.
-   **Raster** data represent a continuous surface as a regular grid of cells: elevation, canopy cover, temperature, predicted density. Handled by **`terra`**, class `SpatRaster`.
-   `terra` also carries its own vector class, `SpatVector`, so raster and vector operations can talk to each other without leaving the package.

::: {.callout-important title="Coordinate reference systems"}
A CRS tells R where on Earth your coordinates sit and what the units mean. Layers must share a CRS before you overlay, clip, or measure. Mismatched CRS is the single most common source of silent spatial errors.
:::

## Old and New Package Names

| Task              | Use this             | Retired                   |
|-------------------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Vector class      | `sf` object          | `sp::SpatialPoints*`      |
| Read vector file  | `sf::st_read()`      | `rgdal::readOGR()`        |
| Reproject vector  | `sf::st_transform()` | `sp::spTransform()`       |
| Raster class      | `terra::SpatRaster`  | `raster::RasterLayer`     |
| Read raster file  | `terra::rast()`      | `raster::raster()`        |
| Reproject raster  | `terra::project()`   | `raster::projectRaster()` |
| Extract at points | `terra::extract()`   | `raster::extract()`       |

::: notes
sp, rgdal, rgeos, and maptools were all retired in October 2023. Any tutorial that leads with readOGR() predates that and will not run on a current install.
:::

## Our Simulated Study Area

A hypothetical 12 × 12 km study area in **UTM zone 12N (EPSG:32612)**, the projection used across western Montana. Coordinates are in **metres**, which means distances and areas come back in sensible units.

| Layer                                | Type         | Built with            |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Survey stations                      | Points       | `sf::st_as_sf()`      |
| Wilderness unit                      | Polygon      | `sf::st_polygon()`    |
| Lost Creek                           | Line         | `sf::st_linestring()` |
| Elevation, canopy, distance to water | Raster stack | `terra::rast()`       |

# Vector Data with `sf`

## Building Points from Scratch

```{r}
library(sf)
set.seed(591)

n <- 25
stations <- data.frame(
  site_id  = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n),
  easting  = runif(n, 280500, 291500),
  northing = runif(n, 5180500, 5191500),
  effort   = sample(20:60, n, replace = TRUE)
)

# Promote the data frame to a spatial object
stations <- sf::st_as_sf(stations,
                         coords = c("easting", "northing"),
                         crs    = 32612)

stations
```

::: callout-note
`st_as_sf()` moves the two coordinate columns into a `geometry` column and leaves every other column as an ordinary attribute. An `sf` object *is* a data frame — `nrow()`, `$`, and `subset()` all still work.
:::

## Inspecting Geometry and CRS

```{r}
class(stations)
sf::st_geometry_type(stations)[1]
nrow(stations)

sf::st_bbox(stations)          # bounding box, in metres

crs_info <- sf::st_crs(stations)
crs_info$epsg              # EPSG code
crs_info$units             # coordinate units
```

## Plotting Points

```{r}
plot(sf::st_geometry(stations),
     pch  = 19,
     cex = 1.3,
     col = "#70002E",
     axes = TRUE,
     main = "Simulated survey stations (UTM 12N)")

box(lwd = 2)
```

Twenty-five stations scattered across the 12 × 12 km study area. Axis values are UTM eastings and northings in metres.

::: callout-tip
`plot(stations)` without `st_geometry()` draws one small panel per attribute column. Wrap in `st_geometry()` when you only want the shapes.
:::

## Reprojecting

```{r}
stations_ll <- sf::st_transform(stations, crs = 4326)

sf::st_crs(stations_ll)$epsg
head(round(sf::st_coordinates(stations_ll), 4), 3)

# Same locations, different numbers
head(round(sf::st_coordinates(stations), 1), 3)
```

::: callout-important
`st_transform()` **reprojects** — it converts the coordinates. `st_crs(x) <- 4326` only **relabels** the CRS without moving anything, which is how layers end up in the Gulf of Guinea. Use the assignment form only when the CRS was recorded wrongly in the first place.
:::

## Building a Polygon

```{r}
poly_coords <- matrix(c(282000, 5182000,
                        289000, 5182500,
                        290000, 5188000,
                        283500, 5190000,
                        282000, 5182000),   # first vertex repeated to close
                      ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

reserve <- sf::st_sf(name     = "Wilderness Unit",
                     geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(poly_coords)), crs = 32612))

# Area comes back in square metres because the CRS uses metres
area_km2 <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(reserve)) / 1e6
round(area_km2, 1)

plot(sf::st_geometry(reserve), 
     col = "#EFE8D4", 
     border = "#1D3C34",
     lwd = 3,
     axes = TRUE,
     main = "Wilderness unit")
plot(sf::st_geometry(stations), add = TRUE, pch = 19, col = "#70002E")
```

The shaded polygon covers roughly 50 km². Maroon dots are the survey stations; some fall inside and some outside.

## Spatial Queries

Which stations fall inside the wilderness unit?

```{r}
hits <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(stations, reserve)) > 0

table(hits)
inside  <- stations[hits, ]
outside <- stations[!hits, ]

plot(sf::st_geometry(reserve),
     col = "#EFE8D4", 
     border = "#1D3C34",
     lwd = 3,
     axes = TRUE, 
     main = "Stations inside versus outside")
plot(sf::st_geometry(outside), add = TRUE, pch = 1,  cex = 1.4, lwd = 2, col = "#333333")
plot(sf::st_geometry(inside),  add = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = "#70002E")
legend("topleft",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Inside", "Outside"),
       pch = c(19, 1),
       col = c("#70002E", "#333333"),
       pt.lwd = 2)
```

::: callout-note
`st_intersects()` returns a list of matches for each feature. `lengths(...) > 0` converts that to a plain logical vector, which is the safest way to subset. `st_within()`, `st_contains()`, and `st_touches()` follow the same pattern.
:::

## Distances Between Points

```{r}
d <- sf::st_distance(stations)                       # 25 x 25 matrix, with units
dm <- matrix(as.numeric(d), nrow = nrow(stations))
diag(dm) <- NA                                   # ignore each point's distance to itself

nnd <- apply(dm, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)

round(summary(nnd), 0)

hist(nnd,
     breaks = 8,
     col = "#DFD1A7", 
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Distance to nearest station (m)",
     main = "Nearest-neighbour distances")
```

Most stations sit within about 1–2 km of their closest neighbour. If you were designing a real array you would compare this against the species' home-range diameter to judge spatial independence.

## Buffers, Union, and Hull

```{r}
buf  <- sf::st_buffer(stations, dist = 1000)   # 1 km around each station
core <- sf::st_union(buf)                      # dissolve overlaps into one shape
hull <- sf::st_convex_hull(sf::st_union(stations)) # smallest convex polygon containing all points

round(as.numeric(sf::st_area(core)) / 1e6, 1)  # sampled area, km2
round(as.numeric(sf::st_area(hull)) / 1e6, 1)  # array footprint, km2

plot(sf::st_geometry(hull),
     border = "#1D3C34",
     lwd = 3, 
     lty = 2,
     axes = TRUE, 
     main = "1 km buffers, dissolved, inside the convex hull")
plot(sf::st_geometry(core), add = TRUE, col = "#BBDDE6", border = "#333333")
plot(sf::st_geometry(stations), add = TRUE, pch = 19, col = "#70002E")
```

The dashed green outline is the convex hull of the array; the pale blue shape is the area within 1 km of any station. The ratio of the two is a rough measure of how completely the array covers its own footprint.

## Lines and Distance to Water

```{r}
stream_coords <- matrix(c(280500, 5183000,
                          284000, 5185500,
                          287500, 5186500,
                          291500, 5190000),
                        ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

stream <- sf::st_sf(name     = "Lost Creek",
                    geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(stream_coords), 
                                          crs = 32612))

round(as.numeric(sf::st_length(stream)) / 1000, 2)     # length in km

stations$dist_stream <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(stations, stream)[, 1])
round(summary(stations$dist_stream), 0)

bin <- cut(stations$dist_stream, breaks = 4)
pal <- hcl.colors(4, "Viridis")

plot(sf::st_geometry(reserve),
     col = "#EFE8D4",
     border = "#1D3C34",
     axes = TRUE,
     main = "Stations coloured by distance to Lost Creek")
plot(sf::st_geometry(stream), add = TRUE, col = "#1F5AA6", lwd = 4)
plot(sf::st_geometry(stations), 
     add = TRUE,
     pch = 19,
     cex = 1.6,
     col = pal[as.integer(bin)])
legend("topleft",
       bty = "n", 
       cex = 0.8,
       title = "Distance (m)",
       legend = levels(bin),
       pch = 19, 
       col = pal)
```

The blue line is the simulated stream. Dark points sit closest to water, light points farthest, and the legend spells out the actual break points so the map does not depend on colour alone. `dist_stream` is now a column you can give to a model as input.

## Reading and Writing Vector Files

```{r}
sf::st_write(stations, "stations.geojson", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
list.files(pattern = "geojson")

stations2 <- sf::st_read("stations.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
nrow(stations2)
sf::st_crs(stations2)$epsg
names(stations2)
```

<!-- ::: {.callout-note} -->

<!-- `sf` reads and writes through GDAL, so shapefiles, GeoPackages, GeoJSON, and KML all use the same two functions. -->

<!-- ::: -->

## Your Turn: Vector Operations

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 6"}
Run the cell, then change the buffer width. How wide does the corridor have to be before half the stations fall inside?
:::

```{r}
library(sf)
set.seed(591)
n <- 25
stations <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(site_id  = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n),
             easting  = runif(n, 280500, 291500),
             northing = runif(n, 5180500, 5191500)),
  coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 32612)
stream <- sf::st_sf(name = "Lost Creek",
                    geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(matrix(c(280500, 5183000, 284000, 5185500,
                                                                     287500, 5186500, 291500, 5190000),
                                                                   ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)), crs = 32612))

# 1. Buffer the stream by 500 m
corridor <- sf::st_buffer(stream, dist = 500)

# 2. Which stations fall inside?
in_corridor <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(stations, corridor)) > 0
sum(in_corridor)

# 3. Map it
plot(sf::st_geometry(corridor),
     col = "#BBDDE6",
     border = "#1F5AA6",
     axes = TRUE,
     main = "Riparian corridor")
plot(sf::st_geometry(stations), 
     add = TRUE,
     pch = 19,
     col = ifelse(in_corridor, "#70002E", "#767676"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The CRS uses metres, so `dist` is given in metres. A 500 m buffer is `dist = 500`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
corridor <- sf::st_buffer(stream, dist = 500)       #<1>
in_corridor <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(stations, corridor)) > 0
sum(in_corridor)                                    #<2>
round(as.numeric(sf::st_area(corridor)) / 1e6, 2)   #<3>
```

1.  Buffering a line produces a polygon 500 m either side of it.
2.  Roughly a quarter of the stations should land inside.
3.  The corridor covers about 16 km² — useful if you need a sampled-area denominator.
:::

# Raster Data with `terra`

## Setup for This Section

The raster examples reuse the three vector layers built in the previous section. If you jumped straight here, or refreshed the page, run this cell first to recreate them.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(sf)
set.seed(591)

n <- 25
stations <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(site_id  = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n),
             easting  = runif(n, 280500, 291500),
             northing = runif(n, 5180500, 5191500),
             effort   = sample(20:60, n, replace = TRUE)),
  coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 32612)

reserve <- st_sf(name = "Wilderness Unit",
  geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix(
    c(282000, 5182000, 289000, 5182500, 290000, 5188000,
      283500, 5190000, 282000, 5182000), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 32612))

stream <- sf::st_sf(name = "Lost Creek",
                    geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(matrix(
                      c(280500, 5183000, 284000, 5185500,
                        287500, 5186500, 291500, 5190000), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)), crs = 32612))

c(stations = nrow(stations), reserve = nrow(reserve), stream = nrow(stream))
```

## Simulating an Elevation Surface

```{r, echo=TRUE}

library(terra)

set.seed(591)

elev <- terra::rast(nrows = 60, 
                    ncols = 60,
                    xmin = 280000,
                    xmax = 292000,
                    ymin = 5180000,
                    ymax = 5192000,
                    crs  = "EPSG:32612")

# Two Gaussian ridges plus noise
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(elev, 1:ncell(elev))
d1 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 284000)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5189000)^2)
d2 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 289500)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5183000)^2)

values(elev) <- 1300 +
  900 * exp(-(d1 / 3200)^2) +
  600 * exp(-(d2 / 2600)^2) +
  rnorm(ncell(elev), 0, 30)

names(elev) <- "elev_m"
elev
```

::: callout-note
`rast()` defines the grid geometry, i.e., extent, resolution, and CRS before any values exist. `values()<-` fills the cells row by row from the top-left. `res(elev)` confirms each cell is 200 × 200 m.
:::

## Mapping the Raster

```{r, echo=TRUE}
plot(elev, 
     col = terrain.colors(50),
     main = "Simulated elevation (m)",
     plg = list(title = "m"))

# Overlay the sf points by converting them to a SpatVector
plot(terra::vect(stations),
     add = TRUE, 
     pch = 19, 
     cex = 1.1,
     col = "#333333")
```

::: callout-tip
`vect()` converts an `sf` object to `terra`'s `SpatVector`; `st_as_sf()` converts back. That pair is how you move between the two packages.
:::

::: notes
Two high ridges rise to roughly 2,200 m and 1,900 m out of a 1,300 m valley floor. Dark points are the survey stations from the previous section.
:::

## Summarising a Raster

```{r, echo=TRUE, include =TRUE}
terra::res(elev)             # cell size, metres
terra::ncell(elev)           # number of cells
terra::ext(elev)             # extent

terra::global(elev, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
terra::global(elev, fun = "range", na.rm = TRUE)

hist(elev,
     col = "#DFD1A7", 
     border = "#333333",
     main = "Distribution of cell elevations",
     xlab = "Elevation (m)")
```

The histogram is right-skewed: most of the study area is valley floor, with progressively fewer cells at higher elevations.

## Map Algebra and a Raster Stack

Rasters behave like numbers — you can add, multiply, and threshold them directly.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
set.seed(591)

noise <- terra::rast(elev)                     # empty raster, same grid
values(noise) <- rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 6)

# Canopy declines with elevation, then is clipped to 0-100%
canopy <- terra::clamp(95 - 0.045 * (elev - 1300) + noise, 0, 100)
names(canopy) <- "canopy_pct"

# Distance from every cell to the stream
stream_v <- terra::vect(stream)
dist_str <- terra::distance(terra::rast(elev), stream_v)
names(dist_str) <- "dist_stream_m"

covs <- c(elev, canopy, dist_str)
covs

plot(covs, col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"), nc = 3)
```

Three panels: elevation, canopy cover, and distance to the stream. All three share the same grid, so they can be stacked and used together.

## Neighbourhoods and Terrain

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# 5 x 5 moving-window mean removes the simulated noise
elev_smooth <- terra::focal(elev, w = matrix(1, 5, 5), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
names(elev_smooth) <- "elev_smooth"

slope <- terra::terrain(elev_smooth, v = "slope", unit = "degrees")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(elev_smooth, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Smoothed elevation (m)")
plot(slope, col = hcl.colors(50, "Inferno"), main = "Slope (degrees)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Smoothing removes the pixel-level noise so `terrain()` returns a realistic slope surface. Steepest values ring the flanks of each ridge; the summits and the valley floor are flat.

::: callout-note
`focal()` is the workhorse for scale questions: change the window size and you change the grain at which a covariate is measured, which often matters more to a habitat model than the covariate itself.
:::

## Reclassifying into Categories

```{r, echo=TRUE}
rcl <- matrix(c(   0, 1500, 1,
                1500, 1900, 2,
                1900, 5000, 3),
              ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

bands <- terra::classify(elev, rcl, include.lowest = TRUE)
levels(bands) <- data.frame(id   = 1:3,
                            band = c("Valley (<1500 m)",
                                     "Montane (1500-1900 m)",
                                     "Subalpine (>1900 m)"))

terra::freq(bands)

plot(bands,
     col = c("#EFE8D4", "#DFD1A7", "#70002E"),
     main = "Elevation bands")
```

`freq()` reports the cell count in each band, and each cell is 200 × 200 m, so multiplying by 0.04 converts directly to km².

## Cropping, Masking, and Resampling

```{r, echo=TRUE}
reserve_v <- terra::vect(reserve)

elev_res <- terra::mask(terra::crop(elev, reserve_v), reserve_v)

# Coarsen from 200 m to 800 m cells
elev_coarse <- terra::aggregate(elev, fact = 4, fun = mean)

res(elev)
res(elev_coarse)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(elev_res, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Clipped to wilderness unit")
plot(terra::vect(reserve), add = TRUE, border = "#1D3C34", lwd = 2)
plot(elev_coarse, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Aggregated to 800 m cells")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

`crop()` cuts the extent down to the polygon's bounding box; `mask()` then sets everything outside the polygon itself to `NA`. You almost always want both.

## Reprojecting a Raster

```{r, echo=TRUE}
elev_ll <- terra::project(elev, "EPSG:4326")

terra::crs(elev_ll, describe = TRUE)$name
round(as.vector(terra::ext(elev_ll)), 4)
round(terra::res(elev_ll), 6)          # now in degrees, not metres

plot(elev_ll,
     col = terrain.colors(50),
     main = "Elevation in longitude and latitude")
```

::: callout-important
Reprojecting a raster **resamples** it: cell values are interpolated onto a new grid, so the result is not identical to the original. Reproject vectors when you can and rasters only when you must, and use `method = "near"` for categorical rasters so classes are not averaged into nonsense.
:::

## Extracting Raster Values at Points

```{r, echo=TRUE}
station_covs <- terra::extract(covs, terra::vect(stations), ID = FALSE)

site_data <- cbind(sf::st_drop_geometry(stations)["site_id"], station_covs)
head(site_data)

# Covariates are correlated - always check before modelling
round(cor(site_data[, c("elev_m", "canopy_pct", "dist_stream_m")]), 2)

pairs(site_data[, c("elev_m", "canopy_pct", "dist_stream_m")],
      pch = 19,
      col = "#70002E")
```

Elevation and canopy cover are strongly negatively correlated by construction, which is exactly the collinearity you would flag before fitting a model with both.

## Writing and Reading Rasters

```{r, echo=TRUE}
terra::writeRaster(elev, "elev.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
list.files(pattern = "tif")

elev2 <- terra::rast("elev.tif")
elev2

all.equal(terra::global(elev, "mean")[1, 1], terra::global(elev2, "mean")[1, 1])
```

::: callout-note
GeoTIFF stores the values, the grid, and the CRS in one file. For a multi-layer stack, `writeRaster()` writes all layers as bands. That is a good reason to name them first.
:::

## Your Turn: Raster Analysis

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 7"}
This mask keeps cells below 1,800 m **and** above 40% canopy cover. Run it, then change either threshold, or swap `&` for `|`, and watch the proportion change.
:::

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(terra)
set.seed(591)
elev <- terra::rast(nrows = 60,
                    ncols = 60,
                    xmin = 280000,
                    xmax = 292000,
                    ymin = 5180000,
                    ymax = 5192000, 
                    crs = "EPSG:32612")
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(elev, 1 : terra::ncell(elev))
d1 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 284000)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5189000)^2)
d2 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 289500)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5183000)^2)
values(elev) <- 1300 + 900 * exp(-(d1 / 3200)^2) +
  600 * exp(-(d2 / 2600)^2) + rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 30)
names(elev) <- "elev_m"
noise <- terra::rast(elev); terra::values(noise) <- rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 6)
canopy <- terra::clamp(95 - 0.045 * (elev - 1300) + noise, 0, 100)
names(canopy) <- "canopy_pct"

# Logical rasters can be combined with & and |
suitable <- (elev < 1800) & (canopy > 40)
names(suitable) <- "suitable"

# Proportion of cells that qualify
global(suitable, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

plot(suitable, col = c("#EFE8D4", "#1D3C34"), main = "Suitable habitat (green)")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Canopy cover is stored as a percentage from 0 to 100, so "more than 40%" is `canopy > 40`. A logical raster holds 0s and 1s, so its mean is the proportion of `TRUE` cells.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
``` r
suitable <- (elev < 1800) & (canopy > 40)           #<1>
names(suitable) <- "suitable"

terra::global(suitable, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE) #<2>
freq(suitable)                                      #<3>
```

1.  `&` combines them cell by cell.
2.  The mean of a 0/1 raster is the proportion of cells that qualify.
3.  `freq()` gives the raw cell counts. Multiply by 0.04 for km², since cells are 200 × 200 m.
:::

<!-- # Putting It Together -->

<!-- ## Workflow -->

<!-- The workflow that runs through the rest of the semester: -->

<!-- 1. Simulate (or load) environmental covariate rasters -->

<!-- 2. Define a true relationship between covariates and occurrence -->

<!-- 3. Sample survey locations and simulate what a field crew would observe -->

<!-- 4. Fit a model to those observations -->

<!-- 5. Predict back across the full raster and map the result -->

<!-- 6. Compare the prediction against the truth you started with -->

<!-- That last step is only possible with simulated data, which is exactly why we start here. -->

<!-- ## Step 1: The True Surface -->

<!-- ``` -->

<!-- psi_hat <- exp(lp) / (1 + exp(lp)) -->

<!-- names(psi_hat) <- "psi_hat" -->

<!-- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) -->

<!-- plot(psi_true, col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"), range = c(0, 1), main = "Truth") -->

<!-- plot(psi_hat,  col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"), range = c(0, 1), main = "Estimated") -->

<!-- plot(pts, add = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "#FFFFFF") -->

<!-- par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) -->

<!-- round(global(abs(psi_true - psi_hat), fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE), 3) -->

<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Both panels use the same colour scale, so they are directly comparable. Mean absolute error across all 3,600 cells is small — the model recovered the surface it was simulated from. -->

<!-- ::: {.callout-tip title="A shortcut worth knowing"} -->

<!-- `terra::predict(covs, fit, type = "response")` does the last step in one call when the raster layer names match the model's predictor names. Doing it by hand once, as above, makes it obvious what `predict()` is actually computing. -->

<!-- ::: -->

# Wrapping Up

## Practice On Your Own

::: {.callout-tip title="Practice"}
1.  Change `set.seed()` in the camera-trap simulation and rerun the summaries. Which conclusions hold and which were noise?
2.  Load one of your own CSV files locally in RStudio. Inspect its dimensions, check the class of every column, and tally observations with `table()`.
3.  Turn your own coordinates into an `sf` object, set the correct CRS, and map them.
4.  Take a real elevation raster for your study area, extract values at your sites, and check for collinearity with `pairs()`.
5.  Simulate a distribution that matches one of your real variables, and overlay the simulated density on your empirical histogram. Which theoretical distribution fits?
:::

<!-- ## Common Errors and What They Mean -->

<!-- | Message | Usual cause | -->

<!-- |---|---| -->

<!-- | `object 'x' not found` | The cell that created `x` has not been run yet | -->

<!-- | `could not find function "st_read"` | `library(sf)` is missing | -->

<!-- | `argument is not numeric or logical` | Applying `mean()` to a character column | -->

<!-- | `st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE` | Layers are in different CRSs — use `st_transform()` | -->

<!-- | `[extent does not overlap]` | Correct CRS, wrong hemisphere or zone | -->

<!-- | `$ operator is invalid for atomic vectors` | Using `$` on a vector or matrix instead of a data frame | -->

<!-- | A `NULL` where you expected data | Misspelled or miscapitalised column name | -->

## Where to Go Next

-   **`sf`** [r-spatial.github.io/sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) has vignettes covering every `st_*` function used here
-   **`terra`** [rspatial.org/spatial-R](https://rspatial.org/) is the reference for raster workflows
-   ***Geocomputation with R*** (Lovelace, Nowosad, Muenchow): free online, the best single text on modern R spatial analysis
-   **R-sig-geo** mailing list: where hard spatial questions get answered

::: notes
Encourage students to bookmark Geocomputation with R specifically. It was rewritten for sf and terra, so unlike much of what surfaces in a search it does not teach retired packages.
:::
